title: On Building Relationships
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Prompted by a colleague's claim that their subject made relationship-building easier, Jo Castelino pushes back on the idea that some teachers are simply gifted at building classroom relationships while others aren't, or that certain subjects lend themselves to it more naturally. She recounts her own past mistake with a demotivated science class -- using games, football chat, and music to build rapport -- which built warm relationships but produced almost no learning and poor assessment results, leaving her mistakenly satisfied because the relationships felt strong. Her revised view is that the relationships that actually motivate learning come from consistency (fair, predictable praise and sanctions), showing students they can be successful (including normalising mistakes as part of learning), and giving students plenty of structured opportunities to practise, rehearse, and retrieve. Over time, this builds trust that the classroom is a place where students can improve and achieve real success -- a different, more durable kind of relationship than one built on shared enthusiasm for football or music during lesson time.
points: Castelino's core reframe -- relationship-building isn't subject-dependent or an innate talent -- directly challenges the colleague's claim that PE simply makes relationships easier to build than other subjects.

Her own cautionary example (a demotivated science class where football chat built warm feelings but 'hardly any learning took place') is a specific, self-critical case study showing that felt rapport and actual learning-supportive relationships are not the same thing.

Her three replacement principles -- consistency, showing students they can succeed, and ample structured practice -- shift the definition of a 'good relationship' from personal warmth to trustworthy, fair, success-generating structure.

The distinction she draws between chatting about students' outside interests during lesson time versus during break/lunch reframes boundary-setting itself as part of what makes a relationship trustworthy for learning, not a barrier to connection.
quotes: Recently, I heard a teacher say how good they were at building relationships in their classroom.
Well, I refuse to believe that only teachers of certain subjects and those somehow blessed with this talent can build a relationship in the classroom.

Despite the limited learning taking place and the poor assessment scores and the fact that my students could barely answer a question correctly, I thought I was doing well because I was building solid relationships.
These are not the relationships that motivate students to learn. My own goal in teaching is to help students love learning.
Students feel belonging when they can trust that the classroom environment is fair, respectful and supportive.
Over time, students start to view the classroom as a place that is fair, where they can improve and achieve hard-earned success.
They won't feel this way if we start talk about football during the lesson, no matter how much they enjoy it in the moment.
